e.etymology: A form of Zilpah, the handmaid of Leah in Genesis and the mother of Gad and Asher. Zelpha is the spelling used in the Latin and Douay-Rheims Bibles.
A spelling of Bertie, the pet form of Bertha, Albert, Herbert and other names built on Germanic beraht, bright. It also overlaps with Birdie.
A respelling of Deborah, Hebrew for bee. In the Book of Judges Deborah is a prophetess and judge who leads Israel to victory.
A variant of Elvira, a Spanish name that goes back to the Visigoths; its original meaning is uncertain.
A spelling of Corene or Coreen, elaborations of Cora, which comes from Greek kore, maiden.
e.note: Looks like an old spelling of Korean.

e.etymology: A Lithuanian name of uncertain meaning, borne by a daughter of Grand Duke Gediminas who became queen of Poland in the 14th century. Lithuanian and Polish immigrants brought it to America.
A German name from Old High German ewa, law or custom, and wald, rule. Two English missionary saints called Ewald were martyred in Saxony around 695.
A clipped spelling of Clarence found in old records. Clarence comes from the English royal title Duke of Clarence, taken from the town of Clare in Suffolk.
A Scottish surname from the town and river of Irvine in Ayrshire, a name thought to be Celtic for green or fresh water. It is a sibling of Irving and Irvin.

assoc.t: Irvine, city in Orange County, California

e.etymology: An American variant of Sonja or Sonia, Russian pet forms of Sophia, Greek for wisdom, with the j said as in English.
A respelling of Judith, Hebrew Yehudit, woman of Judea. In the Book of Judith she saves her city by killing the Assyrian general Holofernes.
A feminine form of Edmond or Edmund, from Old English ead, wealth, and mund, protection. The sculptor Edmonia Lewis, born in the 1840s, is its best-known bearer.
A phonetic spelling of Michaela, the feminine form of Michael, Hebrew for who is like God? It belongs to the wave of Makayla and Mikayla spellings of the 1990s and 2000s.
A respelling of Karen, the Danish short form of Katherine, a name of debated origin long associated with Greek katharos, pure.

assoc.t: often said like Karen, slang for an entitled complainer

e.etymology: Likely a variant of Elmer or Aylmer, both from Old English Aethelmaer, noble and famous.
A pet or feminine form of Clyde, a name taken from the River Clyde in Scotland.
A short form of Sophronia, from Greek sophron, sensible or self-controlled.
A Czech name from Slavic vlast, homeland. In Czech legend Vlasta leads the women's army in the Maidens' War.
An American name built on the -etta ending, as in Loretta and Jeanetta.
A German form of Gerard, from Germanic ger, spear, and hard, brave or hardy. German immigrants brought it to the American Midwest.
A spelling of Trina, the short form of Katrina and Catrina, which are forms of Katherine, a name long associated with Greek katharos, pure.
An elaboration of Cheryl with the French-style -elle ending. It rose in the mid-1980s with the R&B singer Cherrelle, born Cheryl Norton, known for Saturday Love.
The island heroine of Aloma of the South Seas, a 1925 Broadway play filmed in 1926 and again in 1941 with Dorothy Lamour. The name's 1942 peak follows the second film.

A Scandinavian form of the Low German name Helmar, which goes back to older Germanic names such as Hildemar, battle-famed. It also serves as a variant of Hjalmar. Swedish and Norwegian immigrants brought it to the Midwest.
A pet form of Florence and Flora, both from Latin flos, flower.
A short form of Pleasant, the English word used as a virtue-style name for boys in the 19th-century South.
From French chimere, a chimera or fanciful dream. It surfaced as an American girls' name around 1980, when Prince Matchabelli was selling a perfume called Chimere.
A respelling of Lorraine, the region of eastern France, whose name goes back to Lotharingia, the kingdom of Lothar. It became an American girls' name in the early 1900s.
